summary: Mobility is returning to near‑normal levels (MF‑Index 71) while fuel policy remains strong, but actual fuel savings are negligible and high‑risk sectors continue to drive travel. Public transport ridership is recovering to about 86% of pre‑pandemic levels, yet disparities in WFH adoption raise equity and economic concerns. Targeted measures are needed to sustain modal shift and mitigate risk.

signals.detail: The theoretical ceiling of 35.7 million litres saved per week translates to only 334,000 litres actually saved in the first week (~1%), indicating that fuel‑saving benefits of the WFH mandate are currently minimal.
Daily public‑transport trips stand at 1.24 million, roughly 86% of the pre‑pandemic daily average, showing a solid recovery but still short of the 2019 level.
High mobility scores (85‑95) in Retail & Services, Logistics, and Construction—combined with low WFH rates (5‑15%)—signal elevated exposure to congestion, emissions, and productivity losses.
WFH adoption is uneven: Public & GLCs enjoy 60% WFH, while high‑risk private sectors lag at 5‑15%, creating inequitable burden distribution across the economy.
Elevated RON95 price (RM4.32/L) could incentivise a shift to public transport, yet low actual fuel savings and persistent high‑risk travel limit the pace of a durable modal transition.

recommendation: Introduce sector‑specific incentives to raise WFH adoption in Logistics, Construction and Retail to at least 65% within 12 months, coupled with a fuel rebate for public‑transport commuters and subsidies for low‑emission fleet upgrades, to accelerate modal shift and reduce economic risk.
